newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC means business but poorer countries demand role.
newsitem.headline: APEC means business but poorer countries demand role.

text.p: "APEC means business" was the slogan of the fourth annual Asia-Pacific summit, and the private sector is emerging as the glue holding the diverse group of governments together.

The leaders of the 18 member economies of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum wound up their summit on Monday at this former U.S. naval base with a declaration affirming "the central role of the business sector in the APEC process".
A group was set up this year to advise APEC on business matters, underlining the growing role of the private sector in steering APEC's push for economic growth and free trade.
The APEC Business Advisory Council held its first meeting in Manila on the sidelines of the ministerial conference that preceded the leaders' summit.

The leaders' declaration, "From Vision to Action", endorsed the business council's call to facilitate the movement of business people, strengthen investment protection by making contracts more transparent, and involve the private sector in infrastructure planning.
The stakes are enormous.
APEC members account for half the world's population and a mind-boggling $16 trillion in total income. The group accounts for more than 40 percent of global trade.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told reporters at the end of the APEC ministerial conference on Saturday that Philippine President Fidel Ramos "had made a very significant contribution by emphasising that APEC means business".
"Since the very beginning of my own involvement in the APEC process, I've stressed that the critical test of APEC's success is whether it has a practical relevance to the private sector."

The most contentious issue at the Pacific Rim meeting -- a proposal to eradicate tariffs on information technology products by the year 2000 -- actually came out of a group of North American and European business people, U.S. officials said.

The centrepiece of the summit was the actionj plans of individual members for progressively dismantling tariff and non-tariff barriers to create the world's largest free trade and investment region by the year 2020.

"Over the next several years, our Individual Action Plans will produce important openings in each APEC economy -- openings that will mean new opportunities for investment, trade, growth and jobs," Christopher said.

But not everyone in the APEC community, stretching from Australia's Port Arthur to Canada's Prince Edward Island and from China to Chile, is happy with the dash for trade liberalisation, pushed by the business community.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, for one, says level playing fields can be intrinsically unfair.
"A lot has been said about level playing fields," he told the closing session of the APEC business forum on Saturday. "But nothing is said about the size of the contestants."

"Imagine Malaysians playing football with an American team. Two-hundred-fifty pounders on one side and 60-pound Malaysians on the other playing a game we do not know. But we are supposed to play and we are told: 'Look it's fair'."

Non-governmental organisations, protesting on the fringes of the conference, said APEC is building a community where the poor are being excluded, where workers are exploited by multinationals looking for cheap labour and where development is coming at great social and environmental cost.
But businessmen who came here by the hundreds to participate in various Pacific Rim meetings coinciding with the summit said change would be gradual.

While growth would bring pain to some sectors, most would adjust to the change and become stronger for it. In any case, governments can stil intervene to protect local industries and interest groups, they said.
The leaders' declaration also took note of the criticism.
"Promoting rapid economic growth that ensures a healthy environment and improves the quality of life of our citizens is a fundamental challenge," it said.

The declaration also revealed a compromise over the Information Technology Agreement between the proponents of a level playing field and those who say developing countries should be given more time before playing against the big leaguers.

U.S. President Bill Clinton argued for language that would commit leaders to support tariff cuts on information technology products by the year 2000. Malaysia argued that liberalisation in this sector should be flexible to take into account the inability of developing countries to compete in this sector.
In the end, the declaration called for an agreement that would "substantially eliminate tariffs by the year 2000, recognising the need for flexibility".
